paragraphs: Clustering high-dimensional data means finding groups when each observation has many coordinates. This paper asks whether useful recovery is possible even when there are fewer observations than coordinates. Its focus is on sparse cluster centers: the representative vector for each group has only a limited number of nonzero entries.

The authors develop an algorithm that estimates these centers while making just one pass through the data. Their theoretical analysis gives a sample requirement of O(s log d), provided every center is s-sparse in a space with d dimensions. Here, s measures the number of nonzero coordinates in a center, so the stated dependence reflects sparsity rather than the full dimension alone.

This result supports the possibility of accurate center recovery with fewer samples than dimensions when sparsity makes that bound sufficiently small. The single-pass design also addresses computational efficiency. Experiments on several benchmark datasets support both the effectiveness and efficiency of the method compared with the algorithms considered.
icml-2014-a-single-pass-algorithm-for-ef.tldr: A single-pass clustering algorithm can accurately recover sparse high-dimensional cluster centers with a sample requirement of O(s log d).

paragraphs: Representer theorems describe the form an optimal solution can take in a learning problem. In familiar regularization and interpolation settings with Hilbertian penalties, a solution can be expressed as a linear combination of the data. Knowing this form is useful because it ties the search for a solution directly to the observations.

This paper develops a broader framework that brings such results together with analogous optimality conditions from other settings, including matrix regularization. It generalizes what counts as a representer theorem and extends the necessary and sufficient conditions under which one holds. The central connection is to a class of regularization penalties the authors call orthomonotone functions.

The framework includes earlier representer theorems as special cases, while also producing optimality conditions that extend beyond the classical linear-combination form. Its practical conceptual benefit is a criterion for examining a particular penalty: orthomonotonicity helps determine whether the associated regularization problem admits a representer theorem.
icml-2014-a-unifying-view-of-representer.tldr: The paper unifies representer theorems through a property of regularization penalties called orthomonotonicity and derives broader optimality conditions.

paragraphs: Mixed linear regression tries to recover several unknown vectors from measurements whose source is hidden. Each sample comes from one vector, but the learner does not know which. The popular EM approach alternates between assigning samples to vectors and fitting vectors using those assignments. Each iteration is fast, but poor local minima can prevent correct recovery.

The paper introduces an initialization procedure based on the leading two eigenvectors of a suitably constructed matrix. This provides a starting point for EM grounded in the measurements. The authors then analyze a re-sampled version of the algorithm and prove convergence to the correct vectors under assumptions on the sampling distribution.

The guarantee combines successful recovery with nearly optimal sample complexity, meaning the required amount of data is close to what can be achieved for the problem. The abstract reports substantially lower sample requirements than randomly initialized EM and other approaches. The contribution therefore concerns both where the algorithm starts and what can be proved about its subsequent progress.
icml-2014-alternating-minimization-for-m.tldr: A spectral initialization gives re-sampled EM provable recovery and nearly optimal sample complexity for mixed linear regression under sampling assumptions.

paragraphs: Random projections produce transformed data values, but storing those values still requires choosing how many bits to use and what those bits represent. This paper studies how simple coding choices affect similarity estimation and linear classification. The motivation is that a suitable representation can improve both storage requirements and computational speed.

The authors show that uniform quantization outperforms a widely used scheme based on windows and random offsets. They also introduce a non-uniform two-bit code that performs well in their linear support vector machine experiments. These findings support the argument that retaining many bits for every projected value is unnecessary in many cases.

The paper also considers hash tables for approximate near-neighbor search. In that setting, it finds that adding a random offset is unnecessary and can reduce performance. One or two bits per hashed value usually suffice unless the desired similarity level is high. The conclusion is qualified: compact codes can be effective, but the appropriate precision depends on the task and target similarity.
icml-2014-coding-for-random-projections-.tldr: Simple low-bit codes can make random projections more efficient, with one or two bits often sufficient depending on the task and target similarity.

paragraphs: A recommender faces a cold-start problem when a new user or item has little rating history. Active learning addresses this by selecting which initial ratings to request. The paper emphasizes that useful selection requires distinguishing uncertainty about the model from noise inherent in the ratings: an uncertain response is not necessarily an informative one.

The authors propose a Bayesian matrix factorization model for ordinal ratings, meaning ratings whose categories have an order. Its heteroskedastic formulation allows the amount of noise to vary across the data. Alongside the model, they develop a computationally efficient Bayesian active learning framework that uses these uncertainty and noise estimates to choose ratings.

The reported algorithm successfully distinguishes informative observations from noisy ones. The model achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance in the authors' evaluation, and pairing it with active selection yields useful cold-start information from the first requested sample. The contribution connects better rating predictions with a more discriminating way to decide what information to collect next.
icml-2014-cold-start-active-learning-wit.tldr: A Bayesian rating model separates model uncertainty from variable data noise to select informative ratings from the start of cold-start recommendation.

paragraphs: Click-through rate prediction estimates the chance that a user will click an advertisement in a particular context. Logistic regression is widely used for this task because it is straightforward to implement and performs well. However, capturing nonlinear combinations of user and advertisement features is difficult within the standard model.

The proposed coupled group lasso model incorporates conjunction information from user and ad features. This allows the model to account for combinations of characteristics when predicting a click. It also automatically removes features judged unhelpful on both sides. Such feature elimination may make online prediction faster by reducing the information the model needs to process.

To handle large datasets, the authors combine feature hashing with a distributed implementation. Their experiments on real-world data show that the method can achieve state-of-the-art performance on web-scale prediction tasks. The approach brings together interaction modeling, feature selection, and scalable computation, addressing several requirements of advertising prediction within one model.
icml-2014-coupled-group-lasso-for-web-sc.tldr: Coupled group lasso models user–ad feature combinations and removes unhelpful features while supporting web-scale click-through prediction.

paragraphs: One-bit compressive sensing asks how to recover a vector when each measurement retains only a single bit. This paper studies recovery when those highly compressed measurements are also noisy. It develops two algorithms with theoretical guarantees, addressing both ordinary measurement collection and adaptive selection of which measurements to request.

The passive algorithm solves a convex optimization problem with a closed-form solution, making its computation particularly simple. The analysis covers exactly sparse and approximately sparse vectors. For a vector with s nonzero entries in n dimensions, its sample complexity is O(s log n/ε²), where ε is recovery error. This improves the stated previous noisy-setting bound of O(s log n/ε⁴).

When the noise model is known, the authors also propose an adaptive algorithm inspired by active learning. It requests sign information only when the current estimate cannot already infer it. For high-precision recovery, this adaptive method has a lower sample requirement than the passive one. Its advantage therefore comes with an explicit condition: knowledge of the noise model.
icml-2014-efficient-algorithms-for-robus.tldr: Two algorithms recover sparse vectors from noisy one-bit measurements, with adaptive sampling improving high-precision sample efficiency when the noise model is known.

paragraphs: Label propagation uses a graph to extend label information across data points in semi-supervised learning. Computing its optimal labeling scores requires a matrix inverse, with a stated cost of O(n³ + cn²), where n is the number of points and c is the number of labels. This makes the score computation expensive as the dataset grows.

The paper proposes an algorithm that repeatedly calculates lower and upper bounds on labeling scores. These bounds allow it to identify score computations that are unnecessary for deciding the labels and prune them. The key guarantee concerns the resulting labels: they are exactly the same as those obtained from the optimal scores.

The resulting computational cost is O(cnt), where t is the average number of iterations per label. The authors report that t is much smaller than n in practice, and experiments show substantial advantages over existing label propagation methods. The method demonstrates how bounds can preserve exact labeling decisions while avoiding much of the underlying score calculation.
icml-2014-efficient-label-propagation-98.tldr: Iterative score bounds accelerate label propagation while guaranteeing the same labels as the optimal-score solution.

paragraphs: Information can spread through a network whose connections are hidden, leaving only observed cascades as evidence. This paper asks when those traces are sufficient to recover the network, how many are needed, and which structural properties affect the difficulty. It studies a general family of continuous-time diffusion models.

The authors formulate recovery as likelihood maximization with an l1 penalty, which favors sparse connection patterns. They prove that the correct structure can be recovered with high probability from O(d³ log N) cascades when the sampling process satisfies an incoherence condition. Here, N is the number of nodes and d is the largest number of parents of any node.

The bound identifies how the stated sample requirement depends on network size and maximum incoming connectivity, subject to the sampling condition. The paper also develops a simple, efficient soft-thresholding inference algorithm. Experiments illustrate consequences of the theory and show the framework outperforming alternatives in practice, connecting the recovery analysis to an implementable estimation method.
icml-2014-estimating-diffusion-network-s.tldr: An l1-regularized diffusion model recovers network structure with high probability from O(d³ log N) cascades under an incoherence condition.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to average empirical probability distributions using optimal transport. The resulting Wasserstein barycenter is a distribution that minimizes the sum of its Wasserstein distances to the inputs. Through an example, the authors argue that this kind of average has appealing properties that distinguish it from alternatives based on kernel smoothing or Bregman divergences.

They introduce two algorithms whose steps repeatedly need primal and dual solutions to transport problems. These are complementary optimization formulations of the transport calculation. Computing all of those solutions directly is too expensive, so the central computational challenge is making the repeated transport operations affordable.

The authors smooth both formulations to obtain fast approximations of the needed solutions. This connects the barycenter algorithms to a more efficient computational procedure while retaining optimal transport as the basis for the average. Applications include visualizing perturbed images and solving a clustering problem, showing how the proposed averaging machinery can be used in both settings.
icml-2014-fast-computation-of-wasserstei.tldr: Two Wasserstein barycenter algorithms use smoothed transport problems to approximate otherwise expensive repeated optimization steps.

paragraphs: Graph kernels let learning algorithms compare graph-structured objects. Many existing kernels build this comparison from small pieces such as walks, paths, or graphlets. The paper argues that this local perspective misses important global properties, including girth and chromatic number, motivating comparisons that account for the graph as a whole.

The authors introduce two kernels for unlabeled graphs using the Lovász number and its associated orthonormal representation. These mathematical constructions provide a geometric way to capture global graph properties. The paper also proves a result about the kernel's separation margin for classes of graphs, offering theoretical support relevant to choosing a kernel.

Evaluation includes synthetic graphs designed around important global properties and established graph benchmark datasets. The reported classification accuracy is better than or competitive with existing graph kernels. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support global geometric representations as a useful basis for graph comparison, with competitive performance across the evaluated settings.
icml-2014-global-graph-kernels-using-geo.tldr: Two graph kernels use geometric representations to capture global structure and achieve better or competitive classification accuracy in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why a simple unsupervised feature-learning recipe—whitening data and then applying K-means—had performed so well in earlier classification experiments. The broader task is to use unlabeled examples to construct useful vector representations. The authors seek a theoretical explanation for the success of this clustering-based approach.

Their central result links K-means with independent component analysis, or ICA. In the sparse independent-component setting identified by the title, K-means and related clustering methods can recover the ICA mixing matrix or its inverse, the ICA filters. This connects the representation produced through clustering to components already known to provide useful classification features.

The analysis also highlights the importance of whitening, matching the observation from the earlier experiments that this preprocessing step matters. Beyond explaining a successful recipe, the theory leads to an improved initialization for K-means feature learning. The contribution is therefore both an account of why clustering can uncover useful features and a way to improve how that clustering begins.
icml-2014-k-means-recovers-ica-filters-w.tldr: A connection between K-means and ICA under sparse independent components explains the usefulness of whitening-based feature learning and suggests better initialization.

paragraphs: Direct policy search aims to learn controllers automatically, including for tasks with many dimensions. Earlier applications often relied on specialized policy classes with relatively few parameters, restricting their generality. This paper introduces an algorithm for learning more general, high-dimensional policies represented by neural networks.

The method formulates learning as optimization over distributions of trajectories. It alternates between two linked steps: adjusting the policy to match the trajectories, then adjusting the trajectories to match the policy while reducing expected cost. This creates a coupled learning process in which the desired behavior and the controller are repeatedly brought into closer agreement.

The authors report learning policies for difficult control tasks, including recovering from pushes during bipedal movement and walking over uneven terrain, while outperforming prior methods. These results support the use of trajectory optimization to train expressive neural network controllers. The main significance is that the algorithm connects trajectory-level optimization with policy learning in a form capable of handling the complex tasks demonstrated.
icml-2014-learning-complex-neural-networ.tldr: Alternating optimization of trajectories and neural network policies learns controllers for complex tasks such as bipedal push recovery and uneven-terrain walking.

paragraphs: This paper considers a regression function formed by combining k linear classifiers with nonnegative weights that sum to one. The learning problem therefore involves several classifier parameter vectors contributing to a single function. Existing approaches use EM or related procedures, but the abstract identifies a lack of provable guarantees for those approaches.

The authors develop a simple method that combines spectral techniques with a construction they call mirroring. Its stated output is the subspace spanned by the classifiers' parameter vectors. Recovering this subspace identifies the collection of directions containing those vectors, which is a precise structural target within the mixture-learning problem.

Under a probabilistic assumption about the distribution of feature vectors, the authors prove nearly optimal statistical efficiency. This means their method uses an amount of data close to the best achievable for the stated recovery task. The result gives a conditional theoretical foundation for learning this shared parameter subspace, tying the guarantee explicitly to the assumed feature distribution.
icml-2014-learning-mixtures-of-linear-cl.tldr: A spectral method with a mirroring construction recovers a classifier mixture's parameter subspace with nearly optimal statistical efficiency under a feature-distribution assumption.

paragraphs: Correlation analysis helps reveal relationships within data, but the paper notes that most existing measures focus on pairs of dimensions. Its target is relationships involving several dimensions together. The authors argue that discovering such multidimensional patterns calls for a measure designed around multivariate dependence.

They introduce MAC, a multivariate correlation measure belonging to the maximal correlation family. To do so, they generalize maximal correlation analysis to multivariate domains. The paper also examines limitations of existing methods in this family and presents MAC as a way to address them. The central methodological contribution is thus a correlation measure whose scope extends beyond two-dimensional comparisons.

In the reported experiments, MAC outperforms existing solutions, remains robust to noise, and discovers patterns described as useful and interesting. These are empirical findings about the evaluated data and methods. Their significance is that the proposed multivariate formulation supports practical pattern discovery while showing resilience when the observations contain noise.
icml-2014-multivariate-maximal-correlati.tldr: MAC extends maximal correlation analysis to multiple dimensions and empirically discovers useful patterns while remaining robust to noise.

paragraphs: Active learning with Gaussian processes requires deciding which observations to collect. A central difficulty is balancing exploration with exploitation: gathering information and using what is already known must be coordinated. The paper notes that previous approaches mainly made greedy decisions or handled those two objectives separately.

The proposed ε-BAL approach is nonmyopic, meaning it considers consequences beyond the immediate next choice. It jointly optimizes the exploration–exploitation trade-off within an ε-Bayes-optimal formulation. This makes the interaction between present decisions and later learning part of the optimization, rather than treating exploration and exploitation as separate stages of the process.

To support real-time use, the authors derive an anytime algorithm from ε-BAL and provide a performance guarantee. Their experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that it outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms when the available budget is limited. The contribution combines a forward-looking formulation with an algorithm intended for time-sensitive operation, and the evaluation supports its usefulness under constrained learning budgets.
icml-2014-nonmyopic-bayes-optimal-active.tldr: A nonmyopic Gaussian-process active learner jointly optimizes exploration and exploitation, with an anytime algorithm and a performance guarantee.

paragraphs: Spectral methods offer efficient ways to learn latent variable models, but the paper identifies a restriction: existing algorithms largely handle discrete or Gaussian mixture components. The authors propose a kernel method for multi-view models that allows each component distribution to be learned nonparametrically, without supervised component labels.

The method embeds the joint distribution into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and uses a robust tensor power procedure to recover latent parameters. This gives the estimation process a representation that can accommodate flexible component distributions. The sample complexity is quadratic in the number of latent components and a low-order polynomial in other relevant parameters.

The framework also yields, as a special case, an unsupervised conditional density estimator with provable guarantees of the stated kind. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data compare favorably with EM and other spectral algorithms. Together, the results extend tensor-based latent estimation beyond the commonly used component families while retaining favorable sample and computational efficiency.
icml-2014-nonparametric-estimation-of-mu.tldr: Kernel embeddings and a robust tensor power method enable efficient unsupervised learning of multi-view mixtures with nonparametric components.

paragraphs: Content recommendation involves a continuing choice between exploring options and exploiting what has already been learned. Bandit strategies formalize this trade-off. This paper introduces an approach that adaptively clusters such strategies, making the grouping itself part of the online recommendation process.

The authors analyze the algorithm's regret in a standard stochastic noise setting. Regret measures the performance lost through the choices made while learning, so this analysis addresses the cost of exploration as well as recommendation quality. The abstract describes the analysis as sharp and also reports evidence of the algorithm's scalability, connecting its theoretical treatment with its ability to handle larger problems.

Experiments on artificial and real-world datasets show a significant improvement in prediction performance over state-of-the-art bandit methods. These findings support adaptive clustering as a useful ingredient in content recommendation. The contribution combines a new way to organize exploration–exploitation strategies, a conditional regret analysis, and empirical evidence that the organization can improve predictions in the evaluated settings.
icml-2014-online-clustering-of-bandits-3.tldr: Adaptive clustering of bandit strategies improves recommendation predictions in experiments and comes with regret analysis under stochastic noise.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a framework for computation in probabilistic graphical models using the Tensor Train format. This format represents a tensor compactly while supporting efficient linear algebra operations. The authors use those properties to develop methods for working with Markov random fields.

The starting point is a conversion of the field's energy into Tensor Train form. From that representation, the paper addresses two tasks: estimating the partition function and performing maximum a posteriori inference. The partition function provides the normalization needed for probabilities, while MAP inference seeks a most probable configuration. Both tasks are approached through operations on the compact representation.

The authors provide theoretical accuracy guarantees for their partition-function estimation algorithm and compare their methods with several state-of-the-art algorithms. The stated guarantee applies specifically to partition-function estimation. The broader contribution is a computational route from an MRF energy to a representation whose algebraic properties can be used for both normalization and inference.
icml-2014-putting-mrfs-on-a-tensor-train.tldr: A Tensor Train representation of MRF energies supports partition-function estimation with accuracy guarantees and methods for MAP inference.

paragraphs: A model may learn the relationship between inputs and outputs from one input distribution, then make predictions on another. A common response to this covariate shift is to reweight training examples so that they resemble the test population. This paper shows why that adjustment does not always improve test error.

The key issue is whether the chosen model class correctly represents the underlying relationship. The authors analyze changing input distributions as a game between a learner and an adversary, connecting distribution shift with model misspecification. Their analysis characterizes when reweighting is needed, and they introduce robust covariate shift adjustment, or RCSA, to produce relevant weights.

Experiments on UCI datasets and a cancer prognosis dataset support the applicability of the analysis and the effectiveness of RCSA. The main lesson is that weighting decisions should account for the adequacy of the predictive model as well as the difference between training and test inputs. Matching input distributions alone does not settle how well the fitted model will predict.
icml-2014-robust-learning-under-uncertai.tldr: A game-based analysis links covariate-shift correction to model misspecification and yields an algorithm for choosing robust training weights.

paragraphs: This paper compares explicit and implicit stochastic gradient updates for fitting generalized linear models. Its aim is to understand their statistical behavior, including bias, variability, and sensitivity to the learning rate. The authors first develop an efficient algorithm for carrying out the implicit updates in this model family.

They then derive exact formulas for the bias and variance of both procedures. In small samples, the implicit estimates have more bias, but their empirical variance is lower and they are more robust when the learning rate is misspecified. This identifies a trade-off: the implicit method's greater small-sample bias accompanies benefits in variability and robustness.

In the limit, the distinction disappears statistically. Both procedures are unbiased, converge at the same rate, and have the same asymptotic variance. Experiments confirm the theory and suggest that implicit SGD can be competitive for large-scale fitting, especially when robustness matters. The result makes finite-sample behavior a central consideration even when two procedures share the same limiting performance.
icml-2014-statistical-analysis-of-stocha.tldr: Implicit SGD trades greater small-sample bias for lower empirical variance and learning-rate robustness while matching explicit SGD's asymptotic statistical behavior.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification predicts using nearby training examples, so retaining a large dataset can make prediction expensive. Stochastic Neighborhood Compression learns a much smaller synthetic dataset for this purpose. It chooses that dataset to minimize stochastic one-nearest-neighbor classification error on the original training examples.

The compressed representation sharply reduces the amount of data used at prediction time. In the reported experiments, speedups reach several orders of magnitude, and the classifier becomes substantially more robust to incorrect training labels. On four of seven datasets, the compressed version also has lower test error than nearest-neighbor classification using all training data, even at compression ratios as low as two percent.

The speed benefits persist when both approaches use ball trees, hashing, and LMNN dimensionality reduction. This shows that the learned compression can complement those existing acceleration techniques. The findings support synthetic representative data as a way to improve prediction efficiency, with accuracy and noise-robustness benefits in the evaluated cases.
icml-2014-stochastic-neighbor-compressio.tldr: A learned synthetic dataset greatly speeds up nearest-neighbor classification and improves noise robustness, with lower test error on four of seven evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies generative models of source code written and understood by people. Its central idea is that code has both a sequential organization and a hierarchical structure, and a model can incorporate both. The authors describe a family of models designed to represent these aspects together.

A second defining feature is close integration with a compiler. This allows compiler logic and abstractions to help determine the structure built into the model. The authors also develop an extension for generating identifier tokens that takes account of which variables are currently in scope, adding programming-context information to the generation process.

The models can be learned efficiently, and the empirical results show that appropriate structure substantially increases the probability assigned to test programs. That finding concerns how well the models account for observed programs. It supports the value of incorporating compiler-informed organization and scope information into probabilistic code modeling, rather than treating the program solely as a sequence of tokens.
icml-2014-structured-generative-models-o.tldr: Efficient generative code models combine sequence, hierarchy, and compiler-informed scope structure to assign higher probability to test programs.

paragraphs: A basis provides building blocks for representing functions, and the choice of those blocks affects both statistical behavior and computational cost. This paper introduces the falling factorial basis, a spline-like construction with similarities to the classical truncated power basis. The goal is to combine useful function properties with faster calculations.

Its main computational advantage is that multiplication by the basis matrix and basis-matrix inversion can be performed in linear time. The functions are not themselves splines. However, the authors prove that they are sufficiently close to splines to retain some of their favorable properties, giving a theoretical basis for using the new construction.

The paper examines two applications: trend filtering at arbitrary input points and a higher-order version of the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. These connect the same representation to function estimation and distribution comparison. The contribution is a basis whose computational structure supports efficient operations while preserving selected properties associated with spline-based methods.
icml-2014-the-falling-factorial-basis-an.tldr: The falling factorial basis enables linear-time matrix operations while retaining some favorable spline properties for estimation and testing.

paragraphs: Topic models discover themes in document collections, but unsupervised methods can produce topics that lack coherence. Knowledge-based models address this by incorporating prior information supplied by users. This paper develops a way to obtain useful prior knowledge automatically from topics already discovered across many domains.

The approach has two linked components. One mines prior knowledge dynamically during the modeling process; the other is a new topic model that uses that knowledge to guide inference. This connects current topic discovery to information accumulated from earlier collections, without requiring the user to supply domain knowledge for the process.

The authors frame this reuse as lifelong learning: knowledge gained from past data helps with subsequent modeling. Experiments using product reviews from fifty domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The significance is that earlier topic-modeling results become an input to future learning, allowing a growing body of past data and discovered knowledge to inform new topic discovery.
icml-2014-topic-modeling-using-topics-fr.tldr: A lifelong topic-modeling approach automatically mines knowledge from previously discovered topics across domains to guide new topic inference.
